mainTopic: Covering of a broken bone that makes an animal kosher, and the laws of a שליא (placenta)
overview: The amud opens by finishing רבה's lenient ruling about a broken bone covered by sinews that will later harden. רב פפא objects that ריש לקיש disagrees and a Torah איסור is at stake, and רבה falls silent. The גמרא explains why: here רבי יוחנן himself retracted in favor of ריש לקיש. Next comes a real case of a broken, exposed bone with a chip missing. אביי held off ruling, but רבא ruled that it makes no difference as long as most of the bone is covered. The sages then ask what kinds of damaged flesh still count as covering the bone, and they resolve the case of flesh cut like a ring. A new משנה teaches the laws of a שליא found in a slaughtered animal, one that partly came out, and one that was dropped. The גמרא finds a פסוק for the rule and calls part of it an אסמכתא. It then begins a question about a cooked donkey hide, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: רבה's reasons for being lenient
steps.stepSummary: רבה finishes his lenient ruling. He cites רבי יוחנן's rule about registering for sinews for the פסח, and adds that the Torah spares Jewish money.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Sinews that will later harden:] one may be registered for the קרבן פסח on their account. And furthermore, the Torah spared the money of the Jewish people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing רבה's argument for why we need not worry about the sinews over the broken bone. He gives two reasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First reason: according to רבי יוחנן, these sinews count as real meat, since you can join a פסח group just to eat them. So the bone counts as covered by meat. Second reason: the Torah does not want people to lose money for no good reason, which pushes toward leniency.

keyTerms.meaning: One may be registered for them. A person joins a group for the קרבן פסח based on eating this part.
The Pesach offering, which may be eaten only by those registered for it

keyTerms.term: הַתּוֹרָה חָסָה עַל מָמוֹנָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
keyTerms.meaning: The Torah spares the money of the Jewish people (a reason to lean toward leniency)
And furthermore. It introduces an extra reason.

phrases.english: one may be registered on their account for the Pesach offering,
phrases.notes: This finishes רבה's quote of רבי יוחנן: sinews that will harden later count as meat.

phrases.english: and furthermore, the Torah spared
the money of the Jewish people.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִמְנִין עֲלֵיהֶן בַּפֶּסַח, וְעוֹד, הַתּוֹרָה חָסָה עַל מָמוֹנָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבה's ruling, which began before this part of the daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sinews that will later harden count as meat covering the bone, so the animal is permitted. The Torah's concern for Jewish money supports being lenient.

steps.title: רב פפא objects: ריש לקיש disagrees, and this is a Torah prohibition
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא challenges רבה. רבי שמעון בן לקיש disagrees with רבי יוחנן, and the stakes are a Torah-level איסור. So how can רבה brush off the worry? רבה stays silent.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to רבה: But רבי שמעון בן לקיש disagrees, and this is a Torah prohibition, and you say, 'Why worry about them?!' רבה was silent.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא attacks רבה's ruling. Since a major sage disagrees and a Torah law is at stake, we should be strict. רבה gives no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש holds that sinews which will harden are not meat. If he is right, the bone is not covered and the animal is a טרפה by Torah law. When a Torah איסור is in doubt we are strict, so רבה's 'why worry?' seems too lenient. Also, the money reason cannot override a Torah prohibition.

keyTerms.meaning: A prohibition from the Torah itself. When there is a doubt about it, we must be strict.
Why should we worry about them?
He was silent. He had no answer.
An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Rabba:
But Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish [disagrees],
and it is a Torah prohibition,
and you say: Why should we worry about them?!
He was silent.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְרַבָּה: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ, וְאִיסּוּרָא דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's lenient ruling from step 1
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's lenient ruling, which relied on רבי יוחנן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A major sage disagrees, and the doubt involves a Torah איסור, so we must be strict. The money reason cannot outweigh that.
steps.whatToRemember: רבה's silence means he accepted רב פפא's challenge.

steps.title: Why was רבה silent? The הלכה usually follows רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבה did not answer. רבא said the הלכה follows ריש לקיש against רבי יוחנן in only three cases. So רבה could have said the הלכה follows רבי יוחנן here.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why was he silent? But didn't רבא say: the הלכה follows רבי שמעון בן לקיש only in these three cases!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is puzzled by רבה's silence. It points out that he had an easy reply available.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general rule is that when רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש argue, the הלכה follows רבי יוחנן, except in three specific cases. This case is not one of the three. So ריש לקיש's disagreement should not matter, and רבה should have defended his ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: And why? It introduces a question about something that seems unexpected.
The הלכה follows his opinion
Only in these three cases

phrases.english: And why was he silent?
But didn't Rava say:

phrases.aramaic: הִלְכְתָא כְּוָותֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ
phrases.english: the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
[only] in these three cases!
phrases.notes: These are three specific cases listed in יבמות 36a. Everywhere else, the הלכה follows רבי יוחנן.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי אִישְׁתִּיק? וְהָאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רבה's silence in step 2
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's silence in response to רב פפא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The rule for deciding the הלכה favors רבי יוחנן outside three cases, so ריש לקיש's view should not have defeated רבה.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רבה (who was silent) with רבא (who stated the rule about three cases). They are two different sages.

steps.title: Here רבי יוחנן himself retracted
steps.stepSummary: This case is different. רבי יוחנן himself accepted ריש לקיש's view. He told him not to provoke him, since he was teaching the ruling only as one lone sage's opinion.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is different, because רבי יוחנן retracted in favor of רבי שמעון בן לקיש, for he said to him: 'Do not provoke me; I teach it as the view of a lone individual.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why רבה stayed silent. In this case, even רבי יוחנן admitted that his ruling is not the הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual rule of following רבי יוחנן does not apply when he himself backed down. His ruling about sinews was only explaining a minority view, not the accepted הלכה. So ריש לקיש's strict view stands, and רבה had no reply.

keyTerms.meaning: Here it is different. It introduces why the general rule does not apply.
He retracted. He changed his position.
Do not provoke me (with your challenges)
As the view of a lone individual, a minority opinion

phrases.english: Here it is different,
because Rabbi Yochanan retracted
in favor of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish,
for he said to him: Do not provoke me,
I teach it as the view of a lone individual.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי הָכָא, דַּהֲדַר בֵּיהּ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3 and explains רבה's silence in step 2
steps.terutzResolutionType: Exception to the general rule: the author himself retracted
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The usual rule should apply, so the הלכה follows רבי יוחנן and רבה could have answered
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן conceded that his ruling was only a minority view, so ריש לקיש's view stands and רבה had no answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Sinews that will later harden do not count as meat for covering a broken bone, and the animal is forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The rule 'the הלכה follows רבי יוחנן' does not apply when רבי יוחנן himself retracted. Here he did, so the strict view of ריש לקיש stands.
steps.whyThisMatters: In practice, a broken bone covered only by sinews that will later harden is not considered covered by meat.

steps.title: A real case: a broken bone with a small piece missing
steps.stepSummary: A bone broke and stuck out, and a small piece of it fell off. The case came to אביי, who held off ruling for three Festivals.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was a case where a bone broke and stuck out, and a small piece came off it. It came before אביי, and he held off answering for three Festivals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a real-life case. This step sets up the question that the next steps will answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule we know is about a bone that broke and stuck out of the skin. The new twist is that a small piece of the bone came off completely. That made אביי unsure, so he did not rule quickly.

keyTerms.meaning: The bone broke and stuck out through the skin
A small piece or chip
The three pilgrimage Festivals (רגלים)

phrases.english: There was a certain bone that broke and stuck out,
and a small piece was taken off from it.
The case came before אביי,
and he held it off for three Festivals.
phrases.notes: He waited until the sages gathered for the Festivals so he could ask them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא נִשְׁבַּר הָעֶצֶם וְיָצָא לַחוּץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion between רבה and רבי יוחנן/ריש לקיש ended in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no ruling yet. The case is only presented here: a bone broke and stuck out, and a piece of it came off. רבא rules on it in step 7.

steps.title: רב אדא בר מתנא sends the owner to רבא
steps.stepSummary: רב אדא בר מתנא tells the owner to go to רבא בריה דרב יוסף בר חמא, who decides quickly and sharply.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אדא בר מתנא said to him: Go to רבא, son of רב יוסף בר חמא, whose knife is sharp.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short transition line. It sends the case to a different sage and sets up רבא's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי was holding back, so the owner is sent to someone known for deciding quickly. Nothing about the law changes in this step. It only moves the story forward.

keyTerms.meaning: Go
His knife is sharp; he decides cases quickly and sharply

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא:
phrases.english: רב אדא בר מתנא said to him:
Go before רבא,
son of רב יוסף בר חמא,
whose knife is sharp.
phrases.notes: Not a real knife. He means רבא is sharp-minded and rules quickly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַדָּא בַּר מַתְנָא: זִיל קַמֵּיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by sending the open case from step 5 to רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is no ruling here, only a referral to רבא.

steps.title: רבא: it makes no difference whether the piece fell off
steps.stepSummary: רבא reasons from the ברייתא that a broken bone sticking out is kosher when flesh and skin cover most of it. So whether the small piece fell off or not changes nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The owner came before him. רבא said: Since we learned the rule 'the bone broke and stuck out,' what difference is it to me if the piece fell off or if it is still there?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the case from step 5 and rules that the animal is kosher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already deals with a bone that broke and stuck out. It says the animal is kosher if most of the bone is covered. רבא's point is that the bone is already broken and exposed, so a piece falling off adds nothing new. All that matters is whether most of the bone is covered.

keyTerms.meaning: Since; seeing that (opens a line of reasoning)
What difference is it to me? (no real difference)

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבא, once the bone is broken and sticking out, the only question is whether flesh and skin cover most of it. A missing chip changes nothing.

phrases.english: He came before him, and רבא said:
Since we learned 'the bone broke and stuck out,'
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from the previous page (76b): if flesh and skin cover most of the bone, the animal is kosher.

phrases.aramaic: מָה לִי נְפַל, מָה לִי אִיתֵיהּ?
phrases.english: what difference is it to me if it fell off, or if it is still there?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדֵי נִשְׁבַּר הָעֶצֶם וְיָצָא לַחוּץ תְּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the open case from step 5.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the animal kosher if a small piece of the broken, exposed bone came off?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Yes. The ברייתא already covers a broken, exposed bone, so a missing piece makes no difference as long as most of the bone is covered.

steps.title: רבינא asks about flesh that is torn up, crushed, or rotting
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רבא about three kinds of damaged flesh covering the bone: flesh in scattered pieces, crushed flesh, and rotting flesh.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רבא: If the flesh only adds up to a majority when gathered together, what is the law? If it is crushed, what is the law? If it is rotting, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that we know the flesh must cover most of the bone, רבינא asks what kind of flesh counts. These are open questions, and no answer is given here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule says 'flesh covers most of the bone.' Each question tests that rule: Does flesh count if it is in scattered pieces? If it is crushed thin? If it is rotting? The question is whether damaged flesh can still be counted toward the majority.

keyTerms.meaning: Gathered: flesh in scattered pieces that would add up to a majority if put together
Crushed or pulverized flesh
Rotting or decomposing flesh
What is the law?

phrases.english: רבינא said to רבא:
If it adds up when gathered, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The flesh is torn into pieces around the bone, and only together would they cover most of it.

phrases.english: If it is crushed, what is the law?
If it is rotting, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרָבָא: מִתְלַקֵּט מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the rule that flesh must cover most of the bone and asks what kind of flesh counts.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does damaged flesh (scattered, crushed, or rotting) count as covering the majority of the bone?

steps.title: What counts as 'rotting' flesh
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'rotting' flesh means. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע answers: any flesh that a doctor would cut away.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a case of rotting flesh? רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, said: Any flesh that a doctor cuts away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to define one of רבינא's terms, מתמסמס, and gives a clear test for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This step does not answer whether rotting flesh counts toward the majority. It only explains what 'rotting' means. The test is practical: if a doctor would cut this flesh off so the area can heal, it is called rotting.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? How do we picture it?
Doctor
Cuts it away

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא's question is not answered here. רב הונא only explains what 'rotting' means. He does not say whether such flesh counts toward the majority.

phrases.english: What is the case of 'rotting'?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: רב הונא, son of רב יהושע, said:
Any flesh that the doctor cuts away.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָּמֵי מִתְמַסְמֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the third term in רבינא's question from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Any flesh that a doctor would cut away.

steps.title: More open questions about damaged flesh over the bone
steps.stepSummary: The sages raise four more questions about the flesh covering the bone: if it has a hole, is peeled, is cracked, or is missing its bottom third.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was raised: If the flesh has a hole, what is the law? If it is peeled off, what is the law? If it is cracked, what is the law? If its bottom third was removed, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new set of open questions about whether flesh damaged in other ways still counts as covering the bone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These questions continue the line from רבינא's questions. Each one describes a different kind of damage to the covering flesh and asks whether it still counts. 'Bottom third' means the layer closest to the bone is gone, so the flesh is there but not touching the bone.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before the sages
Has a hole in it
Peeled off
Cracked or split
The bottom third

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
If it has a hole, what is the law? If it is peeled off, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the flesh that covers the bone.

phrases.english: If it is cracked, what is the law?
If the bottom third was removed, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The bottom third is the part of the flesh's thickness right next to the bone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: נִיקַּב מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more types of damaged flesh after רבינא's questions in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does flesh with a hole, peeled flesh, cracked flesh, or flesh missing its bottom third still count as covering the bone?

steps.title: Trying to prove from 'skin is like flesh'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings עולא's quote of רבי יוחנן that skin counts like flesh. It hopes this shows that any covering on the bone is good enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: עולא said in the name of רבי יוחנן, skin is like flesh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to answer the open questions about damaged coverings with a known rule: skin counts the same as flesh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If plain skin can count as the covering, then maybe any covering works, even flesh that is not in perfect shape. That would settle the earlier questions in favor of kosher.

keyTerms.meaning: Skin
It is like flesh, it counts the same as flesh

phrases.english: Come and hear, for עולא said
that רבי יוחנן said:
Skin is like flesh,

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר עוּלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer the questions raised in steps 8 and 10.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a covering that is not healthy, full flesh still counts as covering the bone.
steps.raayaSupportSource: עולא quoting רבי יוחנן: skin is like flesh.

steps.title: Maybe the skin there holds tight on its own
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes away the proof. רבי יוחנן may have meant only a spot where skin sits tightly on the bone by nature.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps he meant where the skin holds on by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 11.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's rule could be talking only about a place where the skin naturally hugs the bone and holds on well. That says nothing about damaged flesh, so the earlier questions stay open.

keyTerms.meaning: Perhaps, maybe (used to push away a proof)
Skin, hide
Holds firmly, has a strong grip

phrases.english: Perhaps it is where its skin holds firm on its own.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּלְמָא דִּקְנָה מַשְׁכָּא דִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Full rejection of the proof; the questions stay open.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי יוחנן's rule may only apply where skin naturally holds firmly to the bone.

steps.title: Flesh cut in a ring shape
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports a question from רב פפי's study hall: what if the flesh was cut all around in the shape of a ring?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: When we were in רב פפי's study hall, we asked: if the flesh was cut like a ring, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי brings another question about the covering of a broken bone. This time the flesh is cut in a circle around it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most of the bone is still covered, but the flesh is cut all the way around. The question is whether that cut flesh still counts as a real covering, or whether it is too damaged.

keyTerms.meaning: We had a question, we were unsure
Was cut around in a circle
A ring
What is the law?

phrases.english: רב אשי said:
When we were in the study hall of רב פפי,
we had a question:
If it was cut like a ring, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the flesh and skin around the broken bone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבַּעְיָא לַן: נִקְדַּר כְּמִין טַבַּעַת, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new case of damaged covering, after the earlier questions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does flesh cut all around in a ring still count as covering the broken bone?

steps.title: The doctors say a ring-shaped cut heals
steps.stepSummary: The question was answered from רב's report: the wise men and doctors said you scratch the wound with a bone and it heals. Iron, though, causes swelling.
steps.simpleTranslation: We answered it from what רב יהודה said in the name of רב: I asked the wise men and the doctors about this. They said: scratch it with a bone and it heals, but iron makes it swell.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי tells how they answered the ring question, using what doctors told רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The doctors said this kind of wound can heal when it is scratched with a bone. Since it can heal, the cut flesh still counts as a real covering. They also warn that scratching with iron makes it inflamed.

keyTerms.meaning: We answered it, we resolved the question
Doctors
Scratches it, makes a cut in it
It heals
Iron

steps.confusionAlert: The doctors are giving advice about healing, not a כשרות ruling. The גמרא uses their medical point (this wound heals) to answer the כשרות question.

phrases.english: And we answered it from this
that רב יהודה said in the name of רב:
I asked the wise men and the doctors about this,
and they said: one scratches it with a bone
and it heals,
but iron makes it swell.
phrases.notes: So don't scratch the wound with an iron tool. It will become inflamed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְשַׁטְנָא מֵהָא דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ring-shaped cut can heal (when scratched with a bone), so the flesh still counts as covering.

steps.title: Only when the bone holds its flesh firmly
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא adds a limit: this only works when the bone still holds onto its flesh firmly.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: And that is only where the bone holds its own flesh firmly.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא puts a limit on the answer we just heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wound heals only if the flesh is still firmly attached to the bone. If the flesh is loose, the doctors' healing does not apply, so the answer from step 14 would not hold.

keyTerms.meaning: And that is only when... (adds a condition)
Bone

steps.whatToRemember: Flesh cut like a ring around a broken bone still counts as a covering, because it can heal. But this only works when the bone holds its flesh firmly.

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
And that is where the bone holds its own flesh firmly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: וְהוּא דִּקְנָה גַּרְמָא דִּידֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Puts a condition on the answer of step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The healing (and so the answer) applies only when the bone grips its flesh firmly.

steps.title: A placenta found in a slaughtered animal
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: a שליא found in a slaughtered animal may be eaten by someone who is not disgusted by it. It does not take on טומאת אוכלין or carry טומאת נבלות, unless someone planned to eat it. Then it can get טומאת אוכלין but still not טומאת נבלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone slaughters an animal and finds a שליא in it, a person who is not disgusted may eat it. It does not become impure as food, and it is not impure as a נבלה. If he planned to eat it, it can become impure as food, but it is still not impure as a נבלה.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It teaches the law of a שליא found inside an animal after it was slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The mother's שחיטה makes the שליא permitted, so it is not a נבלה. Most people do not see it as food, so it cannot get טומאת אוכלין. Once a person plans to eat it, his plan turns it into food, so it can now get that טומאה.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה
The placenta, the sac a fetus grows in
A 'hearty soul', someone who is not disgusted
The impurity that food can pick up
The impurity of an animal that died without proper שחיטה
He thought, he planned (to eat it)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of טומאה. טומאת אוכלין is food picking up impurity. טומאת נבלות is the שליא itself being a source of impurity. Planning to eat it changes only the first one.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
One who slaughters an animal
and finds a placenta in it,
a hearty soul may eat it,
phrases.notes: Someone who is not grossed out by eating it.

phrases.english: and it is not impure
neither with the impurity of food
nor with the impurity of carcasses.
If he planned to eat it,
it can become impure with the impurity of food,
but not with the impurity of carcasses.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וּמָצָא בָּהּ שִׁלְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, a new משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שליא found in a slaughtered animal is permitted. It gets טומאת אוכלין only if someone planned to eat it, and it never has טומאת נבלות.

steps.title: A placenta that partly came out is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: If part of the שליא came out of the womb before the שחיטה, it is forbidden to eat. A שליא is a sign of a baby, in a woman and in an animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: A שליא that partly came out is forbidden to eat. It is a sign of a baby, in a woman and in an animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case: a שליא that had partly left the womb before the animal was slaughtered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שליא is a sign that there was a baby in it. Part of it already came out, so we worry the baby counts as already born. Then the mother's שחיטה would not permit it, so the שליא is forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: Part of it
Forbidden to eat
A sign of a baby

steps.whatToRemember: A שליא found inside a slaughtered animal is permitted. But if part of it came out first, it is forbidden, because a שליא is a sign of a baby.

phrases.english: A placenta, part of which came out,
is forbidden to eat,
it is a sign of a baby in a woman
and a sign of a baby in an animal.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁלְיָא שֶׁיָּצְתָה מִקְצָתָהּ – אֲסוּרָה בַּאֲכִילָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception to the permission taught in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שליא that partly came out before the שחיטה is forbidden, since it is a sign of a baby.

steps.title: A dropped placenta from a firstborn or from sacrificial animals
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a שליא dropped by an animal giving birth for the first time may be thrown to the dogs. With קדשים it must be buried. In any case, one may not bury it at a crossroads or hang it on a tree, because of דרכי האמורי.
steps.simpleTranslation: If an animal having its first birth drops a placenta, you may throw it to the dogs. If it is a sacrificial animal, the placenta must be buried. But you may not bury it at a crossroads or hang it on a tree, because those are the ways of the Amorite.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה keeps going and tells us what to do with a שליא that an animal drops. There are two cases: a first-time mother, and a sacrificial animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a first-time mother, we do not worry that the שליא held a holy בכור, so it can go to the dogs. With קדשים the שליא is treated as holy, so it must be buried. The last line forbids burying or hanging it in special places as a good-luck charm, because that copies non-Jewish superstitions.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal giving birth for the first time, whose firstborn could be a holy בכור
Placenta, the sac that holds the baby inside the womb
Sacrificial animals that have been made holy
A crossroads, where two roads meet
The ways of the Amorite: the ban on copying non-Jewish superstitious practices

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that even proper disposal must not be done in a superstitious way.

phrases.english: An animal giving birth for the first time that dropped a placenta
may throw it to the dogs
but with sacrificial animals, it must be buried
and we do not bury it at a crossroads
and we do not hang it on a tree
because of the ways of the Amorite.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמְבַכֶּרֶת שֶׁהִפִּילָה שִׁלְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the same משנה about the שליא that began in steps 16-17
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A first-time mother's dropped שליא may go to the dogs. One from קדשים must be buried. Superstitious burying or hanging is forbidden because of דרכי האמורי.

steps.title: Where do we learn the placenta rule?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source of the משנה's rule that a שליא inside a slaughtered animal is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion with a question: where does the rule about the שליא come from? It is setting up the source that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule in question was taught in step 16: a שליא found inside a slaughtered animal may be eaten. The גמרא wants to know what source teaches it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things known? A standard request for a source

phrases.english: GEMARA: From where are these matters known?
phrases.notes: He means the משנה's rule from before: a שליא inside a slaughtered animal may be eaten.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that a שליא is permitted through its mother's שחיטה

steps.title: The verse includes the placenta, but not if part came out
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the word 'כל' in the פסוק as including the שליא. It reads the word 'אותה' as excluding a שליא that partly came out before the שחיטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Rabbis taught: 'Every... of the animals you may eat.' This comes to include the placenta. You might think this is true even if part of it came out. So the verse says 'it': it, and not its placenta.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא that learns both sides of the rule from one פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The extra word 'כל' widens the permission so that the שליא is included along with the baby. The word 'אותה' narrows it again: once part of the שליא has come out, it is no longer included. This matches both rules of the משנה in steps 16 and 17.

keyTerms.meaning: To include: a word in the פסוק adds a case
You might have thought: brings up a possible mistaken idea
The verse comes to teach: introduces the word that blocks the mistaken idea
Part of it

phrases.english: As the Rabbis taught:
"Every... of the animals you may eat"
phrases.notes: דברים 14:6. Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording, and it matches the פסוק.

phrases.english: to include the placenta.
One might think, even if part of it came out?
So the verse says: "it"
it, and not its placenta.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'כל' includes the שליא. 'אותה' excludes a שליא that partly came out.

steps.title: Why do we need a verse at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא. There is never a שליא without a baby, so a partly-out שליא means the baby may have come out too. Simple logic should forbid it, so why is a פסוק needed?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, there is no placenta without a baby. So why do I need a verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא. It argues that the second half of the rule does not need a פסוק at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 said a שליא is a sign of a baby. If part of the שליא came out, the baby may have come out inside it and counts as born. A born baby is not permitted by its mother's שחיטה, so the שליא is forbidden by logic alone, and the פסוק seems extra.

keyTerms.meaning: Now, after all: opens an argument from something already known
A baby animal, a fetus
Why do I need a verse? Claims a פסוק is not needed

phrases.english: Now, there is no placenta without a baby,
why do I need a verse?

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּדִי אֵין שִׁלְיָא בְּלֹא וָלָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the ברייתא's use of 'אותה'
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's reading of 'אותה ולא שליתה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Logic already forbids a partly-out שליא, because a baby may have come out with it. So the פסוק seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: The verse is only a support
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the פסוק is only an אסמכתא. It is a hint attached to a rule that really comes from logic.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse is just a support.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It agrees the rule comes from logic and says the פסוק is only a hint.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא was not truly learning the rule from 'אותה'. The rule stands on the logic that there is no שליא without a baby, and the פסוק is hooked onto it as a reminder.

keyTerms.meaning: A support: a פסוק used as a hint for a rule that comes from somewhere else
Merely, just

steps.whatToRemember: A שליא inside a slaughtered animal is permitted, learned from 'כל'. If part of it came out, it is forbidden. That second rule really comes from logic, since there is no שליא without a baby, and the פסוק is only an אסמכתא.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the ברייתא is wrong or thrown out. It stays; the גמרא only explains that its second word is a hint and not the real source.

phrases.english: The verse is merely a support.

steps.triggerLanguage: קְרָא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changes how we view the derivation: the פסוק is a hint, not the real source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא learns the ban on a partly-out שליא from 'אותה'
steps.terutzMaskana: The ban comes from logic, and 'אותה' is only an אסמכתא

steps.title: רבי יצחק בר נפחא's question about cooked donkey hide
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'it does not become impure.' It then brings a related question from רבי יצחק בר נפחא: what is the status of a donkey hide that was cooked?
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And it does not become impure.' רבי יצחק בר נפחא asked: a donkey hide that someone cooked, what is its status?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, about the שליא and טומאה. It brings a related question about a donkey hide that was cooked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like a שליא, hide is not normally treated as food. רבי יצחק בר נפחא asks whether cooking the hide changes its status. He does not yet say which kind of טומאה he means.

keyTerms.meaning: Becomes impure or makes things impure
He asked: introduces an open question
The hide (skin) of a donkey
He boiled or cooked it

phrases.english: "And it does not become impure."
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting the משנה from step 16 about the שליא.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nappacha asked:
A donkey hide that one cooked, what is its status?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵינָהּ מְטַמְּאָה. בָּעֵי רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר נַפָּחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a new line of the משנה, about טומאה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The status of a donkey hide that was cooked

steps.title: Which kind of impurity is the question about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the question was about. If it was about טומאת אוכלין, that was already taught in a ברייתא, so it cannot be the point.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what? If it is about food impurity, we already learned that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to pin down what רבי יצחק was asking. It starts by ruling out טומאת אוכלין, which is already known. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A question is only worth asking if the answer is not already known. Since a source already rules on טומאת אוכלין, the question must be about something else. The text continues past this point.

keyTerms.meaning: For what? About which law?
The impurity that food can receive

phrases.english: About what?
If about food impurity, we already learned it,

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמַאי? אִי לְטוּמְאַת אֳכָלִין – תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what רבי יצחק's question was about
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which area of law the donkey-hide question is about, starting by ruling out טומאת אוכלין
